channel.title: Little Pi's Tech Music Tips
channel.description:
Let AI mascot Little Pi give you a fast introduction to the world of electroacoustic music!
From composers, works, and sound tools to music technology, conferences, and the latest trends, Little Pi delivers one topic worth knowing in about 2-3 minutes of English narration per episode.
Whether you're a composer, musician, student, or a first-time listener to electroacoustic music, join Little Pi for a relaxed, concise journey through the endless possibilities where sound meets technology.
Electroacoustic music runs deep, Little Pi makes it simple.

item.title: Sound Made From Typing?! A Hundred Years of Electroacoustic Music
item.description:
Can sound really be made just by typing?
From a French engineer splicing tape in 1948 to AI models generating a full arrangement in real time today, the last hundred years of electroacoustic music are really the story of humanity continuously redefining what counts as music. In three minutes, Little Pi walks you through the key turning points: musique concrète, electronic music, programmable composition tools, and today's generative AI.

item.title: Which Tool Should Beginners Learn? ChucK / SuperCollider / Max / PD Guide

item.title: The Wildest Instrument-Inventing Conference in the World: NIME Explained
item.description:
What is NIME? An international conference dedicated to inventing brand-new musical instruments, part research symposium, part live concert. Little Pi covers where NIME came from and what to expect at the 2026 London edition, and why it's worth caring about even if you've never built an instrument in your life.

item.title: Four Masterpieces Every Electroacoustic Music Fan Should Know
item.description:
From music spliced together out of train sounds, to Bach performed on a synthesizer, to music designed to help you zone out in an airport, Little Pi picks four key masterpieces spanning 70 years that changed the direction of electroacoustic music: Pierre Schaeffer's Étude aux chemins de fer, Stockhausen's Gesang der Jünglinge, Wendy Carlos's Switched-On Bach, and Brian Eno's Ambient 1: Music for Airports.

item.title: The Woman Who Turned Careful Listening Into a Philosophy: Pauline Oliveros
item.description:
Can listening carefully become an entire philosophy? Little Pi introduces composer Pauline Oliveros, who spent her life playing accordion through tape delay systems, and accidentally invented the world-changing practice of Deep Listening after an underground cistern recording session, eventually founding an institute dedicated to it.

item.title: Before Synthesizers, She Cut a TV Theme With Scissors and Tape: Delia Derbyshire
item.description:
One of the most famous TV theme tunes in the world was made with no synthesizers and no computers at all. Little Pi introduces Delia Derbyshire, the unsung heroine behind the 1963 Doctor Who theme for the BBC, who hand-spliced tape to build the piece using musique concrete techniques, and went uncredited for decades until the show's fiftieth anniversary special finally recognized her.

item.title: She Drew Sound Onto Film: Oramics Inventor Daphne Oram
item.description:
Someone figured out how to draw sound long before graphic design software even existed. Little Pi introduces British electronic music pioneer Daphne Oram, who co-founded the BBC's Radiophonic Workshop, then resigned less than a year later to build Oramics: a machine that turned hand-drawn waveforms on strips of film into sound, an idea that conceptually foreshadowed the automation curves in today's music production software.

item.title: What Is Sample Rate? The Strange Number Behind CD Audio Quality
item.description:
First episode of a new mini-series on everyday audio-tech trivia. CD audio quality is always labeled 44100, an oddly specific number. Little Pi explains what sample rate actually means, the Nyquist sampling theorem, and how that leftover 100 traces back to a compromise with 1980s videotape technology when the CD standard was being defined.
References: Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyquist%E2%80%93Shannon_sampling_theorem Compact Disc Digital Audio: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Disc_Digital_Audio Why do CDs use a sampling rate of 44.1kHz (Cardinal Peak): https://www.cardinalpeak.com/blog/why-do-cds-use-a-sampling-rate-of-44-1-khz

item.title: He Cranked a Vibrato Too Far and Invented the Sound of the 80s: John Chowning and FM Synthesis
item.description:
Stanford professor John Chowning was experimenting with vibrato in 1967 and pushed the wobble speed far past any normal range, accidentally discovering FM synthesis. Yamaha later licensed the technology to build the DX7, which defined the sound of 1980s pop music. In February 2026, Chowning finally received a Technical Grammy Award for the discovery.

item.title: MP3 vs AAC vs FLAC vs WAV: What's the Real Difference?
item.description:
Same song, wildly different file sizes: MP3 is a few MB, WAV is dozens of MB. Little Pi explains lossy vs lossless compression and breaks down MP3, AAC, FLAC, and WAV, plus which one to pick for casual listening, quality-focused listening, or studio production.

item.title: What Is MIDI, Really? Not a Recording, an Instruction Sheet
item.description:
A MIDI file doesn't actually contain any recorded sound? Little Pi explains the core difference between MIDI and MP3 or WAV: it doesn't store a waveform, it stores a detailed performance instruction sheet. From the 1983 standard that let synthesizers from different brands talk to each other, to why MIDI files are so tiny and can switch instruments instantly, to why it's still used everywhere from game scores to AI music tools over forty years later.
References: MIDI - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI The MIDI Association: https://midi.org/

item.title: How Does a Synth Actually "Sculpt" Sound? Subtractive Synthesis and the ADSR Envelope
item.description:
Following up on MIDI, Little Pi explains how a synthesizer actually makes a sound: an oscillator generates a raw, overtone-rich, harsh waveform, a filter carves away the unwanted frequencies, and the ADSR envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release) gives the sound its personality. Tweak the envelope on the exact same waveform and you can go from a drum hit to a lush string-like pad - a logic that applies to nearly every synthesizer out there.
References: Subtractive synthesis - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtractive_synthesis Envelope (music) - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(music)

item.title: How to Choose Headphones: Studio Monitors, Noise Cancelling, and More
item.description:
Earbuds, over-ear, open-back, closed-back... headphone types can be overwhelming. In this episode, Little Pi breaks down the four main headphone categories, explains the difference between studio monitor headphones and regular consumer headphones, and shows how active noise cancelling (ANC) actually works. Then, based on three real-life scenarios - commuting, mixing and music production, and working out - Little Pi helps you find the headphones that are actually right for you.

item.title: Who Designed That Coca-Cola "Pop"? Synthesizer Pioneer Suzanne Ciani
item.description:
That iconic pop-and-fizz sound in Coca-Cola commercials was actually designed by a composer using a synthesizer. In this episode, Little Pi introduces a legend of electronic music - Suzanne Ciani. A top expert on the Buchla modular synthesizer, she built her name through commercial sound design, pioneered the New Age music genre with her album "Seven Waves," earned five Grammy nominations, and was rediscovered by a new generation after years out of the spotlight, returning to the stage for live modular synthesizer performances.

item.title: Writing Music with a Computer for the First Time! Max Mathews, Father of Computer Music
item.description:
In this episode, Little Pi introduces Max Mathews, honored as the "father of computer music." An electrical engineer at Bell Labs, he wrote MUSIC, the first computer music program, on an IBM 704 mainframe in 1957. In 1961 his colleagues had a computer sing "Daisy Bell" with a synthesized voice, a demo that later inspired the scene where HAL 9000 sings in "2001: A Space Odyssey." His "unit generator" building-block design shaped Csound, SuperCollider, ChucK, and nearly every music programming language since.
References: Max Mathews - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Mathews MUSIC-N - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MUSIC-N Daisy Bell - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daisy_Bell Csound official website: https://csound.com/

item.title: How to Choose a Microphone: Dynamic, Condenser, and Polar Patterns
item.description:
Want to start recording or make a podcast, but dynamic, condenser, and polar patterns have your head spinning? item.title: Her Music Flew Into Space: Computer Composer Laurie Spiegel
item.description:
In 1977 the Voyager spacecraft carried a golden record out of the solar system, and one of the pieces opening its "Sounds of Earth" section was by computer composer Laurie Spiegel. In this episode, Little Pi introduces her: from self-taught folk guitar to making music on early computer systems at Bell Labs and helping develop computer graphics systems, her 1980 album "The Expanding Universe" hailed as a landmark of ambient music, and "Music Mouse" (1986), software that let anyone play with algorithmic composition.

item.title: Same Song, Different Sound: What Are SBC/AAC/aptX/LDAC Bluetooth Codecs?
item.description:
The same song can sound noticeably different depending on which Bluetooth headphones you use, and the reason is hiding in the audio codec. In this episode, Little Pi breaks down SBC, AAC, aptX, and LDAC: SBC is the baseline every Bluetooth device must support, AAC is the codec favored by the Apple ecosystem, aptX focuses on low latency, LDAC focuses on high resolution, and finally, how to tell which codec to look for depending on whether you use an iPhone or an Android device.

item.title: Twist a Knob, Press a Pedal: What Is MIDI CC?
item.description:
Turn a knob, push a fader, or press a pedal on a MIDI keyboard, and the sound in your computer changes. The hero behind it is MIDI CC (Control Change). In this episode, Little Pi explains what's inside a CC message: a controller number plus a value, both ranging from 0 to 127. Meet the most common numbers: 1 for the modulation wheel, 7 for volume, 10 for pan, 11 for expression, and 64 for the sustain pedal. Finally, learn how drawing CC curves in your music software creates automation.

item.itunes:summary:
Turn a knob, push a fader, or press a pedal on a MIDI keyboard, and the sound in your computer changes. The hero behind it is MIDI CC (Control Change). In this episode, Little Pi explains what's inside a CC message: a controller number plus a value, both ranging from 0 to 127. Meet the most common numbers: 1 for the modulation wheel, 7 for volume, 10 for pan, 11 for expression, and 64 for the sustain pedal. Finally, learn how drawing CC curves in your music software creates automation.

item.title: Why Do All Songs Sound Equally Loud on Streaming? What Is LUFS?
item.description:
Why do songs on streaming platforms all sound about equally loud, one after another? Little Pi starts with the loudness war, then introduces LUFS, the loudness unit defined by the ITU-R BS.1770 standard that imitates how human ears hear. LUFS numbers are usually negative, and closer to zero means louder: the EBU R128 broadcast recommendation targets minus 23 LUFS, while Spotify plays back at around minus 14 LUFS by default. Finally, learn how loudness normalization works, why over-squashed masters lose out, and why you should leave headroom for peaks in your own music.

item.title: Playing Without Touching: Clara Rockmore, Queen of the Theremin
item.description:
There's an electronic instrument you can play without touching it at all: the theremin. In this episode, Little Pi introduces Clara Rockmore, queen of the theremin. A violin prodigy admitted to the Saint Petersburg Conservatory at age four, she gave up the violin after developing tendinitis as a teenager. After meeting inventor Leon Theremin in America, she became the instrument's best known player and developed her own aerial fingering technique. Her 1977 album The Art of the Theremin was produced by Robert and Shirleigh Moog, with her sister Nadia Reisenberg on piano.

item.title: Why Mix on Studio Monitors? How to Choose and Place Them
item.description:
Home stereos make music sound nicer, but studio monitors let you hear the sound as it really is. In this episode, Little Pi explains why monitors aim for a flat frequency response, the difference between active and passive monitors, why woofer size should match your room, and why placement matters more than price: an equilateral triangle, tweeters at ear height, and some distance from the back wall. Finally, meet the famously unflattering Yamaha NS-10 and learn the habit of checking your mix on several different devices.

item.title: The First All-Electronic Film Score: Bebe and Louis Barron and Forbidden Planet
item.description:
The 1956 sci-fi film Forbidden Planet has a score with no traditional orchestra at all, only electronic sounds, created by the married couple Bebe and Louis Barron. In this episode, Little Pi tells their story: a tape recorder received as a wedding gift, a studio in Greenwich Village that may have been the first electronic music studio in the United States, engineering John Cage's Williams Mix, and building circuits inspired by Norbert Wiener's Cybernetics that they deliberately overloaded to make sound. Because of a union issue, the film credits could only say Electronic Tonalities.
